lesson.title: Codes are keys
lesson.subtitle: Two-step sign-in, and the code you never hand over

video.title: Codes are keys
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph in the computer room, telling the story; panels show a game account, a code arriving, a chat asking for it, and the account vanishing.
scenes.animation: Panels slide in one after another with arrows.
scenes.narration: Last month, a student lost his game account. The thief had his password, but the game also asked for a code sent to the student’s phone. So the thief wrote: “Oops, I sent my code to your number. Can you forward it?” He did, and the account was gone.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.narration: Today: two-step sign-in, and why a code is a key you never hand over.

scenes.visual: Two columns: a student passes a password gate and a code gate; a thief passes the first gate and stops at the second.
scenes.animation: The thief bumps into the second gate.
scenes.narration: With two-step sign-in, your password isn’t enough on its own. A new phone signing in also needs a second step: a code, a tap on a prompt, or your fingerprint. A thief with only your password gets stuck.

scenes.visual: Three cards: a thought bubble with stars, a phone, a fingerprint.
scenes.animation: Cards pop in as each is named.
scenes.narration: There are three kinds of proof. Something you know, like a password. Something you have, like your phone. And something you are, like your fingerprint or face. Two different kinds together are much harder to steal.

scenes.visual: A six-digit code turns into a golden key in a student's hand; a friend, a game logo shape and a bank shape all get a no sign.
scenes.animation: The code morphs into a key.
scenes.narration: So here’s the rule. A one-time code is a key for you alone. Nobody real ever asks you to read it out or forward it: not a friend, not the game, not the bank.

scenes.visual: A student and a parent at a phone: email settings, then a chat app's two-step PIN screen, then a game's security page.
scenes.animation: Settings screens slide one by one.
scenes.narration: Turn it on, with a parent if you like, starting with your email: it can reset everything else. In WhatsApp, set a six-digit PIN under Two-step verification. Games and social apps keep it in their security settings.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up a phone with a game chat asking for a code.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A game friend writes: “I sent my code to your phone by mistake. Please send it to me.” What do you do?

scenes.visual: The 'don't send' card gets the check badge; the code on the phone glows as a key to the student's own account.
scenes.narration: Don’t send it. The code came to your phone because someone is trying to sign in to your account. Whoever asks for it wants your account.

scenes.visual: Left: a phone prompt 'Is this you?' with yes and no. Right: a thumb on a fingerprint sensor opens an account, no password box.
scenes.narration: Some apps ask instead: “Is this you signing in?” Only tap yes if it really is you, right now. Passkeys go further: you sign in with your fingerprint or face, so there’s no password to steal.

scenes.visual: A phone falls behind a bus seat; at home a sheet of backup codes sits in a drawer.
scenes.narration: What if you lose your phone? When you turn on two-step sign-in, you’re often given backup codes. Write them on paper and keep them safe at home, not in your phone.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph shows a night-time phone with a sign-in prompt.
scenes.narration: Your turn. At night, your phone asks: “Is this you signing in?” But you’re in bed, not signing in anywhere. What do you do?

scenes.visual: Three summary cards: a shield, a key with a no sign, a notebook.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.on_screen_text: Turn on · Never share · Back up
scenes.narration: Tap no: someone has your password, so change it now. Remember: turn on two-step sign-in, never share a code, and keep backup codes safe at home.

scenes.visual: At home, a student and a guardian turn on two-step sign-in, then fold a paper of backup codes into a drawer.
scenes.animation: Toggle switches on; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: with a parent or guardian, turn on two-step sign-in for your email or WhatsApp. Write the backup codes or the PIN on paper, and keep it somewhere safe at home.

checkpoints.prompt: A game friend writes: “I sent my code to your phone by mistake. Please send it to me.” What do you do?

options.text: Don’t send it — it’s a trick to take my account
Ask them to prove who they are, then send it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a code that arrives on your phone is for your account. Whoever asks for it is trying to sign in as you.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — that code unlocks your account. Your friend’s own account may have been taken over, so call them on their usual number.

checkpoints.prompt: At night your phone asks: “Is this you signing in?” You aren’t signing in anywhere. What do you do?

options.text: Tap yes to make it stop
Tap no, then change your password

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — someone has your password. Saying no blocks them, and a new password locks them out.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — tapping yes lets the thief in. Tap no, change your password and tell an adult.
